pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/kuːˈbɛrə/** ​— ​Sanskrit ‌(IAST: Kubera).[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- ​**Ku-** ‌— ​Short u ‌as ​in ​“put”; ​k ​sharp ​and unaspirated.
- ‌**-be-ra** ​— ‌The ​e ‌is long ​āy-like ‌“ay” ​in ‌careful ​speech: ​Ku-BAAIR-uh. The ‌name ‌is ‌of ​uncertain ​root.
- ‌**-ra** — ​Classical ​Sanskrit ‌stresses ​the ​second ‌syllable: ku-BE-ra; ​the ‌final ​vowel ​is ​short.

​For the ‌modern ‌speaker, ​the ‌closest ​approximation ​is: “koo-BAIR-uh”

‌Kindred ‌and ‌historical ‌forms ​of ‌the name:

- ​**Vedic** ​— ​Vaiśravaṇa
- ‌**Buddhist** ​— Jambhala
- ​**Form** ​— ‌yakṣa-lord
- ​**Pali** ​— ​Kuvera

He ‌began ​as ‌chief ​of ‌the ​evil spirits ‌of ‌darkness ​and ​ended ​as ​the Hindu ‌god ‌of ​riches.

domains.body:
**Kubera** ​is the ‌Hindu god ‌of ​wealth and ​its ​lordly guardian: ​king of ​the ‌yakṣas, the ​treasure-keeping spirits ​of ‌the earth, ​regent ‌of the ​north, and ‌keeper ​of the ​nine treasures. ​From ​a Vedic ​chief ‌of demons ​he rose ‌— ​through Śiva’s ‌favour and ​epic ‌patronage — ​to ‌the dignified ​treasurer of ​the ‌gods, fat, ‌jewelled, and ‌mounted ​on his ​great ‌white guardian-lion ​or his ​human-mule.[^1]

### ‌Lord of ​the North

​One ‌of the ​four ‌lokapālas, regents ​of the ​directions; ​his quarter ​is the ‌north, ‌seat of ​wealth.

### ‌King of ​the Yakṣas

​The ‌treasure-spirits of ‌earth serve ‌him; ‌his capital, ​Alakā, ‌gleams on ​Mount Kailāsa’s ​flank.

### ​The Nine ‌Treasures

Nidhi, ​the ​nine jewels ​of ‌kingship, lie ​in his ​keeping ​— each ‌a named ​power ‌of abundance.

### ​The ‌Money-Pot

His ​mongoose ejects ‌jewels ‌from its ​mouth in ​Buddhist ​form; his ​belly ‌is the ‌vault he ​guards.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Kubera ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- **Lord ​of ​the ​North** ​— ‌One ​of ‌the four ​lokapālas, ‌regents ​of ‌the ​directions; ‌his quarter ​is ​the ‌north, ‌seat ‌of ​wealth.
- ​**King of ‌the ​Yakṣas** ​— ‌The ​treasure-spirits ​of ‌earth serve ​him; ‌his ​capital, ​Alakā, ​gleams ​on ‌Mount Kailāsa’s ‌flank.
- ​**The ‌Nine ​Treasures** ​— ‌Nidhi, ‌the nine ‌jewels ‌of ​kingship, ‌lie ​in ​his keeping ​— ‌each ​a ​named ​power ‌of ​abundance.
- **The ​Money-Pot** ​— ‌His ​mongoose ‌ejects ​jewels ‌from its ​mouth ‌in ‌Buddhist ​form; ​his ​belly ​is the ‌vault ‌he ​guards.

mythology.body:
Kubera’s mythology ​is a success ‌story: the demon-chief who ‌became a god. ​The Veda knows ​him only as ​Vaiśravaṇa, the powerful one ​of the dark; ​the epics made ‌him the friend ​of Rāma’s line, the ​builder of Laṅkā ‌before Rāvaṇa took ​it, and the guardian ‌whose aerial chariot ​Pushpaka still serves ‌the righteous.[^1]

### The ​Lord of Laṅkā Before ​Rāvaṇa (Rāmāyaṇa)

Kubera ​built the golden ​city of Laṅkā ​on the world’s far ‌shore, served by ​the yakṣas and ‌filled with his ​hoard. His half-brother Rāvaṇa, ‌through austerities and ​violence, took the ‌city and the ​flying chariot Pushpaka from ‌him; Kubera withdrew ​north to mount ​Gandhamādana, and Laṅkā ‌passed to the demons ‌— the great ‌city’s golden age ​remembered as his.[^2]

### The ​Aerial Car Pushpaka ‌(Mahābhārata)

The epic’s ​greatest vehicle belonged ​to Kubera: the self-moving ‌palace-car Pushpaka, won ​back from Rāvaṇa ​by Rāma and ‌returned in the epic’s ​closing book to ‌its maker’s friend. ​To ride Pushpaka ​is to command the ​wealth of the ​world from above ‌— and Rāma, ‌refusing it, set the ​moral: treasure serves, ‌the righteous decline ​it.

### The Demon Who ​Won a God’s ‌Favour (Śiva Cycle)

‌The Purāṇas tell ‌how Kubera, in an ‌earlier cosmic round, ​performed austerities until ‌Śiva granted him ​guardianship of the north ​and lordship of ​wealth. Some tellings ‌begin him darker: ​a gluttonous yakṣa king ​whose eye was ​burnt by Paraśurāma’s ‌glance — the ​scar that marks his ​images’ asymmetric face.

### ​Jambhala, the Buddha’s ‌Treasurer (Buddhist Transformation)

​Buddhism adopted him outright ‌as Jambhala — ​black or golden, ‌eared with the mongoose ​that spits gems, ‌seated on a ‌citron fruit. In ​this form he became ​the wealth-god of ​Tibetan and Himalayan ​Buddhism, his mantras ‌recited in monasteries that ‌formally renounce what ​he provides.

overview.body:
**Kubera** (*kubera*) ​— Riches, ‌the Northern ‌Quarter · ​Originally a ​chief of ​the evil ​spirits of darkness, ​bearing the ‌name Vaiśravaṇa ​— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the domain ‌"Wealth, Treasure, ​North". The ​name means ​"Originally a ​chief of ​the evil ‌spirits of darkness, ​bearing the ‌name Vaiśravaṇa; ​in later ‌mythology the ​god of ‌riches and ​treasure, regent of ‌the northern ​quarter."[^1].

**Kubera** ​is the ‌Hindu god ‌of wealth ‌and its ​lordly guardian: ​king of the ‌yakṣas, the ​treasure-keeping spirits ​of the ‌earth, regent ​of the ​north, and ‌keeper of the ​nine treasures. ‌From a ​Vedic chief ​of demons ​he rose ​— through ‌Śiva’s favour and ‌epic patronage ​— to ‌the dignified ​treasurer of ​the gods, ‌fat, jewelled, ‌and mounted ‌on his great ‌white guardian-lion ​or his ‌human-mule.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical scholarly ​spelling **Kubera** ‌and serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/kubera/). ​The displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed from the ‌displayed form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *kubera* ‌contains the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ‌diacritics or special ​encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**कुबेर**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Originally ​a chief ‌of ​the evil ​spirits ‌of darkness, ​bearing ‌the name ​Vaiśravaṇa; ‌in later ​mythology ​the god ​of ​riches and ​treasure, ‌regent of ​the northern ‌quarter."[^1].

​The canonical ‌spelling ​**Kubera** matches ‌the ​conventional scholarly ‌romanization. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *kubera* ‌contains ‌the same ​letters, ​so no ‌lost diacritics ​or ​encoding transition ‌is ​claimed. The ​editorial ‌work is ​to ‌fix one ​reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, and ‌keep ​the original ‌evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ‌form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ‌description ​computed from ‌the ​displayed form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**k** ​→ **K** ​— ‌Same
- **u** ​→ ​**u** — ​Short ‌/u/
- **b** ​→ ‌**b** — ​Same
- ‌**e** → ​**e** ‌— Short ‌/e/
- **r** ​→ ​**r** — ​Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ‌— Short ​/a/
